data.content_ref: inline:The claim commits a category error by conflating falsifiability (a logical property measuring how much a theory rules out) with corroboration (an empirical record of surviving severe tests). The claim states we choose the better-corroborated theory 'specifically because it is more falsifiable,' but in Popperian epistemology these are distinct dimensions. A maximally falsifiable theory that has never been tested has zero corroboration; a less falsifiable theory that has survived many severe tests can have high corroboration. Popper's critical convention is to prefer the theory with the greater degree of corroboration, not the greater degree of falsifiability per se. The 'specifically because' clause misstates the Popperian rationale: we prefer the better-corroborated theory because it has survived more severe tests, not because it is more falsifiable. The mechanism itself shifts to a different justification ('maximizing learning velocity'), which is a pragmatic/strategic ground distinct from both corroboration and falsifiability, revealing that the claim's stated reason (falsifiability) does not match its own defense (learning velocity).
